description: 3 friends from the University of Bristol in 2nd year, studying Physics and Engineering.
summary: We have created a website for analysing different lunar landing sites and finding the best site for set mission parameters from a dataset of over 80,000 candidate landing sites. Users can select a site by clicking on the 3D Moon model or entering the latitude and longitude. Our dashboard shows information about the landing sites selected. The Sun and Earth visibility can be seen on the time-adjustable graph along with the angle to the local horizon, showing when the Sun and Earth would be visible. We also display an image of the landing site, nearby sites of scientific interest, and a route between them which has the most scientific potential within the travel distance specified. Sites are given a score for safety (calculated through how rough and steep the potential landing area is), a score for science (based on the value of the sites you can reach), a score for solar power generation (based on Sun visibility throughout the mission timeline), and a score for Earth visibility (for finding communications windows). The user can select the weights for these individual scores using sliders or by describing the mission parameters to an AI assistant, and these are used to find a total score for the landing site. The landing sites are then ordered and the scores for each are shown next to the time graph with a marked landing site photo. You can also search through our dataset of candidate sites to find the 5 with the highest score to display data for.
details: Lunar Navigator (live at https://lunar.isaacbarker.net/, with source code athttps://github.com/Theo7c/Lunar-landing-site-nav; please note that because the backend uses free-tier hosting, initial requests may be slow to respond) is an interactive lunar landing-site dashboard that helps users identify, evaluate, and compare candidate landing sites anywhere on the Moon. On the frontend, users configure a Mission Window with start and end timestamps, define spacecraft Capabilities including maximum rover travel distance, a return-to-lander toggle, and lander presets (such as Standard Exploration Lander) that adjust landing footprint size and slope tolerance, and select candidate locations by entering coordinates, choosing historic or polar presets like Apollo 15, Apollo 17, Chang'e 5, or Shackleton Crater, or clicking directly on an interactive 3D textured Moon. Users can adjust four priority sliders for Safety, Solar Power, Direct Earth Contact, and Scientific Interest and click Search All Sites to populate the top 5 highest-scoring locations across the Moon, or describe their mission in plain English to an integrated Google Gemini AI assistant (gemini-3.5-flash-lite) that automatically generates weights and engineering justifications. Selected sites appear as color-coded pins on the 3D globe matched to ranked comparison cards displaying overall and individual 0-to-1 scores, coordinates and elevation, a rendered 2D hillshaded topographic route map, and dual time-series graphs plotting Sun (orange) and Earth (blue) elevation angles against the local terrain horizon (grey dotted line). A synchronized timeline scrubber along the bottom sweeps through the mission window to update live Sun and Earth elevation readouts and reveal when the Sun or Earth drops below the local horizon across all compared sites simultaneously. Under the hood, a FastAPI backend evaluates every site across four normalized metrics combined into a weighted Multi-Criteria Decision-Making score. For terrain safety, it extracts local elevation, maximum and mean slopes across the touchdown footprint, and surface roughness (including a 2 km EVA mobility roughness window for precomputed South Pole sites) from dual-tier NASA LRO LOLA Digital Elevation Models—using an 80 m/px South Pole stereographic DEM (LDEM_80S_80MPP_ADJ) below 80 degrees South and the global LDEM_64 (~474 m/px) dataset elsewhere—enforcing hard lander slope and roughness limits while scoring remaining safety margins. For scientific value, it queries a 3D Moon-centered Cartesian (cKDTree) catalog of Sites of Scientific Interest combining roughly 1,500 large NASA PGDA Permanently Shadowed Regions and roughly 10,000 sub-kilometer micro-PSRs capable of trapping water ice with curated Artemis polar ridges, lava tube skylights, Irregular Mare Patches, volcanic pyroclastic vents, magnetic anomalies, farside basins, and historic benchmarks. Within the chosen rover range, a greedy plus 2-opt orienteering solver computes the highest-value multi-stop traverse route of up to 20 stops, scored via exponential distance decay and a half-saturation curve, while an on-the-fly renderer generates a 2D hillshaded DEM map displaying the true-to-scale landing dispersion zone, nearby and visited science targets, the optimized rover path, and a dynamic scale bar. For solar power and Earth communications, the backend ray-casts 360-degree local horizons out to 80 km using exact spherical lunar curvature geometry and compares them against topocentric Sun and Earth ephemeris angles fetched from the NASA JPL Horizons API over the selected mission window to calculate exact visibility fractions. This replaces complex GIS workflows and manual ephemeris parsing with an accessible, transparent browser tool that supports early-stage Artemis and CLPS mission trade studies—letting users rapidly test scenarios like nuclear power, relay satellites, or higher lander slope tolerances—while making real NASA planetary datasets tangible for education. Creatively, Lunar Navigator pairs natural-language AI accessibility and synchronized multi-site time scrubbing with 100% deterministic planetary physics, normalizing polar water-ice cold traps and global geological features onto a single 1.0-to-5.0 intrinsic value scale so polar and non-polar missions compete fairly. Key engineering factors considered by our team include exact spherical lunar curvature (R = 1737.4 km) in 80 km horizon ray-casting, cosine-latitude distortion in global slope and equal-area sampling, longitude normalization to [-180, +180] across mixed planetary datasets, distinct touchdown footprints (250 m polar vs. 710 m global), square-root PSR area scaling so massive craters like Shackleton do not drown out smaller rover-reachable micro-PSRs, and 3D spatial deduplication when merging catalogs. To keep the app responsive, an offline pipeline precomputes roughly 60,000 candidate landing zones (30,000 dense South Pole sites, 30,000 equal-area global sites extracted via patch-based sampling to avoid 265M-pixel full-array convolutions, and 12 featured landmarks) alongside 360-degree horizon profiles cached in binary .npz files for fast single-site lookups, while batch ranking uses fast local analytical visibility estimates before running live JPL Horizons queries and optional remote NASA TIFF streaming (/vsicurl/) on demand for selected coordinates. The project is built with Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Rasterio/GDAL, Matplotlib, Requests, the Google Gemini API (google-genai), and an interactive 3D web dashboard, powered by NASA LRO LOLA LDEM_64, NASA PGDA South Pole DEM (LDEM_80S_80MPP_ADJ) and PSR catalogs (LPSR_80S_20MPP_ADJ), Braden et al. (2014) Irregular Mare Patch data, and the NASA JPL Horizons Ephemeris API.
